idiom_name: internal token type with an internal constructor; the assembly is the grant (InternalsVisibleTo admits one friend assembly)
implementation_notes: C# has no friend-to-type: the accessibility domain of a private member is the program text of the type that declares it (C# specification, accessibility domains), and the spec's own example shows that a nested type's private members are not reachable from the enclosing type - so the Java-style nested key cannot be built. What C# provides instead is scope: mark the key class and its constructor internal and any code in the assembly can mint one, or move the key and the restricted type into their own assembly and admit exactly one friend assembly with [assembly: InternalsVisibleTo]. File-scoped types (C# 11) are narrower still, but a file-local type cannot appear in the signature of a non-file-local type, so they cannot carry a public operation. The token still documents the seam and supports delegation, but the grant is assembly-sized: treat it as a build boundary plus readability, not as per-type access control.
pitfalls: Assembly scope is visible to every type in the assembly, and InternalsVisibleTo hands over the whole internal surface rather than one collaborator.
Porting the Java shape does not work: a nested key's private constructor is not callable from the enclosing type, so the enclosing type cannot mint keys.
Reflection (Activator.CreateInstance on a non-public constructor) reaches the key at run time; the boundary is compile-time only.
